01.text: Investigators, journalists, lawyers and researchers share one problem.

02.text: Too much evidence to read, and a result nobody can later prove was not changed.

03.text: Sealbook is an app for exactly that. It works in three steps.

04.text: You bring the material in. The app reads all of it and proposes connections, each shown with the exact place it came from.

05.text: A person approves or declines each one with a signature, and the record is sealed, so anyone can check it later.

06.text: Four invented cases show how that helps.

07.text: One: a freight company pays a supplier, a consultant, a guarantor and a ship agent. Four desks, four clean files.

08.text: Kassar. Qassar. Khassar. Kasar. And on one licence, the name in Arabic.

09.text: Four spellings, two alphabets, one man. And one who is not him: a surveyor with the same name, born elsewhere.

10.text: The app proposed these links, each with the passage behind it. Fixed rules with no AI model found 4 of the 6 true links, enough to join all his records.

11.text: A person declines the surveyor, and signs each decision with a passkey, a key on their own device.

12.text: The case closes on a conclusion, signed by a person and checked by a colleague: one man, on four desks, under four names.

13.text: Two: a workshop burns down at night. The bookkeeper says she spent the evening at her sister's house, 34 kilometres away.

14.text: The app flags that two exhibit sheets made from her own phone place her at the workshop that same day.

15.text: Three: a flood video spreads as breaking news.

16.text: Four: a nurse boards a night bus and is never seen again.

17.text: Every decision is signed by a person. A court can check the sealed package offline; here, on a test package.

18.text: The machine reads more than a person can, and finds the links. A person approves every one.

07b.text: Are these four people, or one man under four names?
07b.note: cut from a longer take; the spoken figure 1,445 was misheard as 1,045, so the numbers stay on screen only

13b.text: Was she? There are 41 statements to read.

14b.text: A person reads the times, 21:52 and 22:07, and concludes she was there.

15b.text: Is it new? The tip line holds 36 clips that look alike.

15c.text: The app compares their sound and ties the viral clip to a video posted two years earlier. It had been cropped and mirrored, so the picture no longer matched.

15d.text: 8 of 9 reposts were tied this way. One muted copy is missed. A person signs that the clip is old.

16b.text: Where do you look? The bus company's logs run to several hundred lines.

16c.text: A supervisor's statement says when the driver was last seen. From that night, the app finds 73 days in which no log names him.

16d.text: A person records it as a lead to follow, not a finding.
